tagline: An old turnpike connects Guilford’s green with the road to Durham.
intro: Route 77 leads from Guilford’s town green through North Guilford into Durham, with state scenic designation along its entire length. The drive passes Lake Quonnipaug on the way inland. A separate 1.4-mile scenic section of Route 17 continues through Durham, from Route 77 to just north of Route 68. Guilford’s green is framed by churches and civic buildings; Durham’s western side is flanked by the traprock heights of the Metacomet Ridge.

In 1824, the road between the two town centers was chartered as the private Guilford and Durham Turnpike. Connecticut took over its main through roads in 1922, incorporating the old alignment into State Highway 112. In 1932, the portion south of Durham center became Route 77. Its original southern end was US 1; the extension to Route 146 followed in 1962.

Start on Whitfield Street at the green, follow its west side, then leave on Church Street. Beyond US 1 and I-95, the road becomes Durham Road. The Route 80 junction provides connections toward Killingworth and North Branford before the road crosses into Durham. Across the Durham town line it becomes Guilford Road and ends at Route 17 just south of the center.
notice: At Guilford’s green, Route 77 follows the west side before leaving on Church Street.

moments.title: Guilford Green
moments.text: The green occupies 7.7 acres in Guilford’s historic district, with churches, shops and the town hall along its edges. Nearby on Union Street, the Sabbathday House preserves a shelter for churchgoing families. Colonial churchgoers attended morning and afternoon Sunday services. Families traveling long distances needed somewhere to rest between them. The town allocated land for these shelters, and as many as thirty were built. This house is one of two that survive in Guilford. The house’s roof combines a gambrel front with a rear shed roof, above wooden clapboards and an irregular pair of front windows.

moments.title: Lake Quonnipaug
moments.text: Route 77 passes Lake Quonnipaug in northern Guilford. Guilford’s largest lake has a 41-acre park with a pavilion, picnic tables and a supervised beach.

moments.title: Durham
moments.text: Durham’s Main Street follows a ridge between swampy areas, a layout that limited the street grid. The agricultural town’s center benefited from travelers between Hartford and New Haven, with taverns and other services along their route. Shoemaking developed as a cottage industry in the early nineteenth century. Its civic buildings changed use, too: the town hall occupies a Greek Revival church built in 1849. The historic district also includes a library built in 1901. The district’s houses span Federal and Victorian styles and include simpler buildings constructed for mill workers, alongside the more elaborate residences.
